Thought: To solve this problem, we need to identify which elements have valence electrons in both the s and d sub-levels in their ground state electron configurations. These elements are typically transition metals, as they have partially filled d orbitals. Let's examine each element:

- Cl (Chlorine) has the electron configuration [Ne] 3s² 3p⁵. Its valence electrons are in the s and p sublevels, not d.
- Cr (Chromium) has the electron configuration [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹. It has valence electrons in both the 4s and 3d sublevels.
- F (Fluorine) has the electron configuration [He] 2s² 2p⁵. Its valence electrons are in the s and p sublevels, not d.
- Mn (Manganese) has the electron configuration [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s². It has valence electrons in both the 4s and 3d sublevels.
- Na (Sodium) has the electron configuration [Ne] 3s¹. Its valence electrons are only in the s sublevel.
- Ni (Nickel) has the electron configuration [Ar] 3d⁸ 4s². It has valence electrons in both the 4s and 3d sublevels.

The elements Cr, Mn, and Ni have valence electrons in both the s and d sublevels.
